qs.q: A 77-year-old man has a routine check-up. The only finding is slight nodularity of his prostate on digital rectal examination. Serum PSA is 6 ng/mL. A prostate biopsy shows prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN). Which of the following is the best medical care option to offer this man?
qs.e: PIN is a potential precursor of prostatic adenocarcinoma, but by itself does not warrant therapy.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) is a premalignant lesion of the prostate epithelium, identified on biopsy. It signals increased risk of prostate cancer and guides surveillance. Clinicians must integrate histology with PSA trends and patient factors.

sections.p: PIN is a microscopic abnormality of prostatic ducts and acini, characterized by nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, and architectural disarray without stromal invasion. Diagnosis requires prostate biopsy and histopathologic review.

t.b: Detects PIN; absence of invasion confirms non‑malignant status.

t.a: Immunohistochemistry for basal cell markers (e.g., p63, CK5/6)
t.b: Positive basal cells rule out carcinoma; negative basal cells support PIN.

sections.p: PIN is graded as low‑grade (LG‑PIN) or high‑grade (HG‑PIN). HG‑PIN carries a higher progression risk to adenocarcinoma. No formal TNM staging applies, but extent of involvement guides follow‑up intensity.

The exact etiology is unclear, but chronic inflammation, hormonal imbalance, and genetic alterations (e.g., PTEN loss) are implicated. In low‑resource settings, infections such as schistosomiasis or chronic prostatitis may contribute.

Patients are usually asymptomatic; PIN is often discovered incidentally during evaluation for elevated PSA or during prostate biopsy for other reasons. Rarely, it may coexist with prostatitis symptoms.
Key investigations confirm diagnosis and assess cancer risk. When resources are limited, focus on biopsy and basic PSA testing.

t.b: Elevated PSA raises suspicion for PIN or cancer; trend over time informs surveillance.
Detects nodularity or asymmetry; normal DRE does not exclude PIN.
Histology confirms PIN; number of cores and distribution guide follow‑up.

sections.p: Progression to prostate cancer is the main complication. Rapid PSA rise, new DRE abnormalities, or increasing PIN burden warrant prompt re‑biopsy.

whenToSeekHelp: Symptoms of urinary obstruction or pain

faq.a: No, PIN is a premalignant lesion; it does not invade surrounding tissue but increases cancer risk.

faq.q: Do I need treatment for PIN?
faq.a: No active treatment is needed; surveillance with PSA and repeat biopsy if indicated is standard.

faq.q: Can lifestyle changes reduce PIN progression?
faq.a: Healthy weight, exercise, and controlling infections may lower progression risk, but evidence is limited.
